Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Any form of physical contact with others

I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette:
Aisha, a 74-year-old African American woman, had spent her entire life working the rich soil of her family’s farm, but the earth that once sustained her now held a different, darker meaning. It had been seven years since the late afternoon when she was accosted in a secluded patch of the fields, the air thick with the scent of damp soil and drying hay, the silence of the setting sun broken only by the rustle of leaves. That day, her sense of self, her body, and her world were irrevocably altered.

Now, the very smells of soil and outdoor air, once comforting, had become potent reminders, triggering a cascade of distress. Even the sudden, complete silence that sometimes fell over the fields at dusk, or in her quiet home, would send a jolt of terror through her, pulling her back to that moment. When these triggers arose, Aisha’s first instinct was to force herself to think only positive thoughts, a desperate attempt to push away the encroaching dread. This strategy, however, often left her feeling disingenuous, deepening her conviction that her life was not worth living anymore, a painful appraisal that echoed in her quiet moments.

The anniversary of the event, in particular, plunged Aisha into a profound despair, reinforcing her belief that she was dirty or contaminated because of what had happened to her body. This deep-seated feeling of contamination and body shame made her recoil from any form of physical contact with others, including her loving partner, with whom intimacy had become a source of profound discomfort and guilt. Her partner’s gentle touch, meant to offer comfort, would instead trigger a wave of shame, making her pull away and further internalize the belief that she was somehow tainted. This avoidance of touch, while providing a fleeting sense of safety from perceived re-traumatization, only served to deepen her conviction that her body was irrevocably damaged and shameful, reinforcing the very negative appraisals she desperately tried to escape.

As the years passed, Aisha’s conviction that her body was shameful and contaminated became a lens through which she viewed the world, making her increasingly vigilant for any reminder of the trauma. This heightened sensitivity meant that even mundane outdoor smells or moments of quiet, which she might have once dismissed, now registered as intense triggers, expanding the scope of what she had to avoid. For Aisha, it felt as though the world itself was conspiring to remind her of her humiliation, and her only recourse was to withdraw. She began avoiding circumstances that reminded her of the event, particularly being in the dark or working alone in the quieter parts of the farm, even though this impacted her ability to carry out her duties effectively. Each path she now deliberately avoided on the farm, each quiet corner she steered clear of, became a new marker of the trauma, subtly expanding the mental map of what could potentially trigger her. These avoidance behaviours, meant to protect her from further distress, paradoxically intensified her negative appraisals, as each successful avoidance prevented her from experiencing that the world was not always dangerous, and that she was not inherently contaminated.

The cycle tightened around Aisha, her life shrinking to accommodate her fears. Her efforts to force positive thoughts grew more exhausting, failing to genuinely lift the cloud of despair. The more she avoided physical contact, the more isolated she felt, and the more she believed her life wasn't worth living. The constant vigilance, the shame, and the pervasive sense of contamination had become her constant companions. It was the growing distance from her partner, a man she loved dearly but could no longer bear to be touched by, and the encroaching dread of each new anniversary, that finally brought Aisha to seek help. She was tired, weary of the fight, and desperately hoped there was a way to reclaim the life she once knew, before the earth and its silence became her tormentors.
